newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Tyremaker Michelin's profits rise, stock skids.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tyremaker Michelin's profits rise, stock skids.

text.p: Tyre giant Michelin on Tuesday reported a five percent rise in profits in 1996 but the modest gain masked a jump in results excluding exceptional charges.
Its stock slid, however, as the results were lower than anticipated and the extraordinary charges greater than expected.
Cie Generale des Etablissements Michelin, which vies with Japan's Bridgestone for the top global ranking, said net profit rose to 3.11 billion francs ($545 million) from 2.96 billion.

Stripping out exceptional charges of 845 million francs, profit climbed to 3.96 billion francs last year from 2.89 billion, helped by record sales volumes, lower rubber prices and financial expenses, and favourable currency trends.

The group's performance was boosted by rapid sales gains in emerging markets and brisk business in replacement tyres in the United States that helped offset slow growth in U.S. and European car production and downturns in the truck industry.
Sales volumes grew 6.4 percent last year, and turnover rose to 71.25 billion francs from 66.11 billion.
Operating profit climbed to 6.96 billion francs from 5.70 billion in 1995, approaching the minimum target of 10 percent of sales, Finance Director Eric Bourdais de Charbonniere said.
"That's the minimum if we want to compete with Goodyear and Bridgestone," he told a news conference. The three companies together hold more than half of the global market.

The 1997 results should "confirm the favourable trend of recent years," Bourdais de Charbonniere said. Michelin put in place a big cost-cutting programme in 1993, and last year reorganised its businesses to speed up its response to market shifts.

Its 1996 charges included 1.15 billion francs to cut jobs in Spain and France. Bourdais de Charbonniere said the group needed to trim staff to stay globally competitive but was trying to do so gradually to avoid shocks.

Michelin also took an unexpected 750 million franc charge to cover its exposure to a private bank, Banque Industrielle et Mobiliere Privee, in which it holds a 38 percent stake. "That was a bolt from the blue," said one analyst.
The charges overwhelmed a 964 million franc gain generated largely from the sale by Michelin of a 2.6 percent stake in carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen in December.
The exceptional items narrowed the gain in net attributable profit, which rose to 2.89 billion francs from 2.80 billion in 1995. The market had expected a figure closer to 3.4 billion.

Michelin's stock was down 3.42 percent at 328 francs in afternoon trading. Brokers said investors were disappointed in the results and heavy charges, but noted that the share has rallied more than 20 percent since the start of the year.
Big improvements in the balance sheet, which was marred by the acquisition of U.S.-based Uniroyal-Goodrich seven years ago, had been largely expected.

Michelin said it cut its debt by 3.4 billion francs to 22.8 billion francs last year. Debt had stood over 35 billion francs in 1993. The group recently announced the early redemptions of convertible bond issues expected to total five billion francs.
Michelin said in its earnings statement that it expected its efforts to cut costs and financial expenses, encourage innovation and penetrate new markets to help 1997 results.
Net investment is expected to rise to more than five billion francs in 1997 from 4.1 billion last year.
The group is studying possible acquisitions in emerging markets, expected to show the biggest growth in tyre sales in coming years, Bourdais de Charbonniere said.
"We're looking at several dossiers in emerging markets," he said, adding that "none of them are of a size that would constitute a major acquisition".

Michelin said it expected the tyre market to broadly follow the pattern seen in 1996. "The tyre markets in 1997 should experience a growth scenario similar to that of 1996, weaker in the developed markets of Europe, North America and Japan than in the emerging markets," it said.
($ = 5.704 French Francs)
